story.title: The heart that ran out of oxygen

scenes.text: A coronary artery blocks. Within seconds, heart muscle cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.
After 20–40 minutes, some damage becomes irreversible.
What changes inside the cell?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Reversible vs irreversible
steps.body:
**Reversible**: ATP falls → Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails → cellular swelling (hydropic change), ER swelling, membrane blebs, fatty change, clumped chromatin.
**Irreversible** (point of no return): severe mitochondrial damage, membrane rupture, lysosomal enzyme leak, nuclear changes — **pyknosis** (shrinkage), **karyorrhexis** (fragmentation), **karyolysis** (fading).

steps.title: Types of necrosis
steps.body:
- **Coagulative**: architecture preserved, ghost cells — infarcts of heart, kidney (not brain).
- **Liquefactive**: brain infarcts, abscesses.
- **Caseous**: cheese-like, in tuberculosis (granulomas).
- **Fat necrosis**: acute pancreatitis (saponification), breast trauma.
- **Fibrinoid**: immune vasculitis, malignant hypertension.
- **Gangrenous**: limb ischaemia (dry) ± infection (wet).

**Apoptosis**: programmed, energy-dependent, single cells shrink, chromatin condenses, apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed — **no inflammation**. Caspases execute it (intrinsic mitochondrial pathway via BCL-2 family and cytochrome c; extrinsic via Fas/TNF receptors).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying brain infarcts show coagulative necrosis — they liquefy.
- Saying apoptosis causes inflammation — it typically does not.

lessons.title: Lab: Order the events of acute inflammation

scenes.text: A splinter in a gardener's finger becomes red, hot, swollen and painful within hours.
Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor — and loss of function.
Put the events in order.

steps.title: Vascular and cellular events
steps.body:
1. Transient vasoconstriction, then **vasodilation** (histamine, prostaglandins) → redness, heat.
2. **Increased permeability** (endothelial contraction) → protein-rich exudate → swelling.
3. Stasis → **margination** of leukocytes.
4. **Rolling** (selectins), **firm adhesion** (integrins binding ICAM-1), **transmigration** (PECAM-1/diapedesis).
5. **Chemotaxis** (C5a, LTB4, IL-8, bacterial products).
6. **Phagocytosis** (opsonins C3b, IgG) and killing (oxidative burst via NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase).

steps.title: Defects
steps.body: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 = defective integrin (CD18): delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent infections without pus. Chronic granulomatous disease = NADPH oxidase defect: infections with catalase-positive organisms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up selectins (rolling) and integrins (firm adhesion).
- Calling a transudate an exudate — exudate is protein- and cell-rich due to increased permeability.

steps.title: Granulomatous inflammation
steps.body:
A **granuloma** is a collection of activated macrophages transformed into **epithelioid cells**, often with **multinucleated giant cells** (Langhans type), rimmed by lymphocytes. Driven by Th1 cells (IFN-γ activates macrophages).

- **Caseating**: tuberculosis (also some fungi).
- **Non-caseating**: sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, foreign body, leprosy (tuberculoid), berylliosis.

steps.title: Healing
steps.body:
**Primary intention** (clean, apposed edges): minimal granulation tissue, thin scar. **Secondary intention** (large gap, infection): abundant **granulation tissue** (new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells), **wound contraction** by myofibroblasts, larger scar.

Sequence: haemostasis → inflammation (neutrophils, then macrophages) → proliferation (granulation tissue, angiogenesis by VEGF, collagen type III) → remodelling (type III replaced by type I collagen; strength ~70–80% of normal by about 3 months).

Delayed by infection, diabetes, poor nutrition (vitamin C, zinc, protein), steroids, poor blood supply.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the scar regains full strength — it rarely exceeds about 80%.
- Forgetting keloid is excess collagen extending beyond the wound margin.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- **↑ Hydrostatic pressure**: heart failure, venous obstruction (DVT).
- **↓ Plasma oncotic pressure**: nephrotic syndrome (protein loss), cirrhosis (less albumin), malnutrition.
- **Lymphatic obstruction**: filariasis, cancer surgery/radiation → lymphoedema (non-pitting with time).
- **↑ Permeability**: inflammation, burns (exudate).
- **Sodium retention**: renal failure, RAAS activation.

- Forgetting that inflammatory oedema is an exudate (protein-rich), the others are transudates.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — DVT and pulmonary embolism

scenes.text: A 45-year-old woman on oral contraceptives returns from a 12-hour flight with a painful swollen calf.
Two days later she is suddenly breathless with chest pain.
Work through it.

steps.title: Virchow's triad
steps.body:
1. **Endothelial injury** (surgery, trauma, atherosclerosis).
2. **Abnormal blood flow** — stasis (immobility, long flights) or turbulence.
3. **Hypercoagulability** — inherited (factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency) or acquired (pregnancy, oestrogen-containing pills, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome).

Thrombus fates: propagation, embolisation, dissolution, organisation and recanalisation. **Lines of Zahn** (alternating platelets/fibrin and red cells) indicate a thrombus formed in flowing blood (ante-mortem).

steps.title: Embolism
steps.body: Most pulmonary emboli arise from **deep veins of the leg** above the knee. Large emboli can cause sudden death (saddle embolus); smaller ones cause infarction mainly when the bronchial circulation is compromised. Other emboli: fat (long-bone fractures), air, amniotic fluid, tumour, septic.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Sudden breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency — call 112. Suspected PE needs immediate senior review, risk scoring and imaging; anticoagulation is started by the treating team.

steps.title: Types of shock
steps.body:
- **Hypovolaemic**: haemorrhage, dehydration, burns — low preload; cold peripheries.
- **Cardiogenic**: MI, arrhythmia, myocarditis — pump failure; raised JVP, pulmonary oedema.
- **Obstructive**: massive PE, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade.
- **Distributive**: septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic — vasodilation; warm peripheries early in sepsis.

Stages: non-progressive (compensated) → progressive (tissue hypoperfusion, lactic acidosis) → irreversible (multi-organ failure).

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: Anaphylaxis needs intramuscular adrenaline promptly by trained staff per protocol and a 112 call outside hospital.

steps.title: Red vs white infarcts
steps.body:
- **White (anaemic) infarcts**: solid organs with **end-arterial** supply — heart, kidney, spleen.
- **Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts**: organs with **dual** circulation or loose tissue (lung, liver), venous occlusion (testicular or ovarian torsion), or reperfusion of a previously ischaemic area; also small intestine.

lessons.title: Benign vs malignant and naming tumours

scenes.text: A 25-year-old finds a mobile, rubbery breast lump; a 60-year-old finds a hard, fixed one.
Biopsy: fibroadenoma in the first, carcinoma in the second.
What separates benign from malignant?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Features
steps.body:
**Benign**: well differentiated, slow growth, encapsulated, no invasion, **no metastasis**.
**Malignant**: variable differentiation (anaplasia — pleomorphism, high N:C ratio, hyperchromasia, atypical mitoses), rapid growth, **local invasion**, **metastasis** (the definitive feature).

Naming: benign epithelial — adenoma/papilloma; malignant epithelial — **carcinoma**; benign mesenchymal — -oma (lipoma); malignant mesenchymal — **sarcoma**. Exceptions: lymphoma, melanoma, seminoma are malignant despite '-oma'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every '-oma' benign.
- Confusing hamartoma (disorganised normal tissue) with choristoma (normal tissue in the wrong place).

lessons.title: Lab: Sort oncogenes and tumour suppressors

scenes.text: A child has retinoblastoma in both eyes; his father had it too.
One faulty copy was inherited; the second was lost in the eye.
Learn the genes behind cancer.

steps.title: Two classes
steps.body:
**Oncogenes** (gain of function, one hit enough): RAS (point mutations), MYC (amplification/translocation — Burkitt t(8;14)), HER2/ERBB2 (amplification in breast cancer), BCR-ABL (t(9;22) in CML), BRAF (melanoma).
**Tumour-suppressor genes** (loss of function, both copies — Knudson's two-hit): RB (retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma), TP53 (Li–Fraumeni), APC (familial adenomatous polyposis), BRCA1/2 (breast, ovarian), NF1, WT1.

steps.title: Hallmarks of cancer
steps.body: Self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to growth inhibitors, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replication (telomerase), sustained angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, reprogrammed metabolism (Warburg effect), evasion of immune destruction — enabled by genomic instability and tumour-promoting inflammation.

scenes.text: A 62-year-old man has smoked bidis for 40 years and chews tobacco.
He now has a non-healing ulcer on the side of his tongue.
Work it up.

steps.title: Carcinogens
steps.body:
- Tobacco (smoked/chewed): lung, oral cavity, larynx, oesophagus, bladder, pancreas.
- **Aflatoxin B1** (Aspergillus on stored grains/peanuts): hepatocellular carcinoma (TP53 mutation).
- **HPV 16/18**: cervical, oropharyngeal, anal cancers (E6 inactivates p53, E7 inactivates RB).
- **Hepatitis B/C**: hepatocellular carcinoma. **EBV**: Burkitt, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. **H. pylori**: gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
- **Asbestos**: mesothelioma, lung cancer. **Aromatic amines** (dyes): bladder. **Vinyl chloride**: hepatic angiosarcoma. Ionising radiation: leukaemia, thyroid cancer.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: Any mouth ulcer or white/red patch lasting more than 2–3 weeks, especially in tobacco users, needs examination and biopsy by a doctor or dentist. Quitting tobacco lowers risk; Tele-MANAS 14416 and national quitlines can support quitting.

steps.title: Common markers
steps.body:
- **AFP**: hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumour.
- **β-hCG**: choriocarcinoma, some testicular germ cell tumours.
- **CEA**: colorectal (follow-up), others.
- **CA-125**: ovarian epithelial cancer.
- **PSA**: prostate cancer (also raised in benign enlargement and prostatitis).
- **CA 19-9**: pancreatic cancer.

Spread: carcinomas favour **lymphatic** spread; sarcomas favour **haematogenous** spread (exceptions: renal cell carcinoma, HCC, follicular thyroid cancer and choriocarcinoma spread via blood).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using markers as screening tests for the general population without indication.
- Assuming a normal marker excludes cancer.

scenes.text: A pale 24-year-old woman's report: Hb 9 g/dL, Hct 30%, RBC 4.0 million/µL.
The machine has printed MCV, but your examiner wants you to calculate it.
Do it by hand.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Solved example · Indices
steps.body:
- **MCV** (fL) = Hct (%) × 10 ÷ RBC (millions/µL) = 30 × 10 ÷ 4.0 = **75 fL** (microcytic; normal ~80–100).
- **MCH** (pg) = Hb (g/dL) × 10 ÷ RBC = 9 × 10 ÷ 4.0 = **22.5 pg** (hypochromic; normal ~27–32).
- **MCHC** (g/dL) = Hb ÷ Hct × 100 = 9 ÷ 30 × 100 = **30 g/dL** (low; normal ~32–36).

steps.title: Classify by MCV
steps.body:
- **Microcytic**: iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease (sometimes), sideroblastic.
- **Normocytic**: acute blood loss, haemolysis, chronic kidney disease, anaemia of chronic disease.
- **Macrocytic**: B12/folate deficiency (megaloblastic), alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Hct as a fraction (0.30) in the MCV formula that expects a percentage.
- Calling every microcytic anaemia iron deficiency — check iron studies and think of thalassaemia trait.

lessons.title: Lab: Iron deficiency vs thalassaemia trait

scenes.text: Patient A: heavy periods, Hb 9, MCV 72, RBC 3.8 million.
Patient B: well, Hb 11.5, MCV 64, RBC 5.9 million; his sister has the same.
Sort their findings.

steps.title: Iron studies
steps.body:
- **Iron deficiency**: low ferritin (best single test), low serum iron, **high TIBC**, low transferrin saturation; high RDW; pencil cells.
- **Anaemia of chronic disease**: low iron, **low/normal TIBC**, normal or **high ferritin** (acute-phase reactant, hepcidin ↑).
- **β-thalassaemia trait**: normal iron studies, high RBC count for the Hb, very low MCV, **raised HbA2 (> 3.5%)** on HPLC; Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC) < 13 suggests trait.

steps.title: Solved example · Mentzer index
steps.body:
A: 72 ÷ 3.8 = **18.9** (> 13 → favours iron deficiency).
B: 64 ÷ 5.9 = **10.8** (< 13 → favours thalassaemia trait). Confirm with ferritin and HbA2.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Iron should not be given blindly to thalassaemia carriers. Carrier screening and genetic counselling before marriage/pregnancy help prevent thalassaemia major.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — haemolysis and sickle cell disease

scenes.text: A 16-year-old from a tribal area of central India has severe bone pain and jaundice.
Hb 7, reticulocytes high, indirect bilirubin high.
Work it up.

steps.title: Haemolysis and sickle cell
steps.body:
Haemolysis markers: ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin; intravascular haemolysis also gives haemoglobinuria. Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test separates immune from non-immune causes.

**Sickle cell disease**: point mutation in β-globin (glutamate → valine at position 6) → HbS polymerises when deoxygenated → sickled cells → **vaso-occlusive crises**, haemolysis, autosplenectomy (infection risk with encapsulated bacteria), acute chest syndrome, stroke. Prevalent in parts of central and western India among some tribal communities. Diagnosis by HPLC/electrophoresis; sickling test for screening.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Severe pain, fever, breathlessness, chest pain or neurological symptoms in sickle cell disease need urgent hospital care.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Bioavailability (F)**: fraction of the dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged (IV = 1). Reduced by poor absorption and **first-pass metabolism** (gut wall and liver — e.g. oral nitroglycerin, lidocaine, propranolol).
- **Volume of distribution (Vd)** = amount in body ÷ plasma concentration. Large Vd = drug in tissues (e.g. chloroquine, digoxin); small Vd = stays in plasma (e.g. warfarin, heparin).
- **Clearance (CL)**: volume of plasma cleared per unit time.
- **Half-life**: t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL. Steady state is reached after about **4–5 half-lives**.
- **First-order kinetics**: constant fraction eliminated per unit time (most drugs). **Zero-order**: constant amount (ethanol, high-dose phenytoin, high-dose aspirin).

steps.title: Metabolism
steps.body: Phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis — CYP450) and Phase II (conjugation: glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation). **Enzyme inducers**: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, chronic alcohol, St John's wort. **Inhibitors**: macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azole antifungals, cimetidine, grapefruit juice, ritonavir. **Slow acetylators** are more prone to isoniazid neuropathy and drug-induced lupus with hydralazine/procainamide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Vd with a real anatomical volume — it is a theoretical value.
- Forgetting that rifampicin reduces the effect of oral contraceptives (risk of contraceptive failure).

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Affinity**: how well a drug binds. **Efficacy (intrinsic activity)**: how big a response it produces once bound.
- **Potency** (EC50): dose needed for 50% of max effect — curve position. **Efficacy** (Emax): height of the curve.
- **Full agonist**: maximal response (morphine at µ). **Partial agonist**: submaximal even at full occupancy (buprenorphine at µ). **Inverse agonist**: opposite effect to an agonist on constitutively active receptors.
- **Competitive antagonist**: shifts curve right, Emax unchanged (naloxone, atropine). **Non-competitive/irreversible**: lowers Emax (phenoxybenzamine).
- **Therapeutic index** = TD50 ÷ ED50 — narrow for digoxin, lithium, warfarin, phenytoin, aminoglycosides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating potency with efficacy — a more potent drug isn't necessarily more effective.
- Forgetting partial agonists can act as antagonists in the presence of a full agonist (buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal).

steps.title: Receptor map
steps.body:
- **M2** (heart): ↓ HR. **M3** (glands, smooth muscle, eye): secretion, bronchoconstriction, gut motility, miosis, accommodation, bladder contraction.
- **Nicotinic NM** (neuromuscular junction), **NN** (ganglia, adrenal medulla).
- **α1**: vasoconstriction, mydriasis (radial muscle), bladder neck contraction. **α2**: presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release (central sympatholytic effect).
- **β1**: ↑ HR and contractility, renin release. **β2**: bronchodilation, vasodilation in muscle, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis, K⁺ into cells.

steps.title: Mechanism and features
steps.body:
Organophosphates **irreversibly** inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ACh accumulates.
- **Muscarinic**: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis, sweating.
- **Nicotinic**: fasciculations, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis; tachycardia/hypertension possible.
- **CNS**: confusion, seizures, coma.

steps.title: Treatment principles
steps.body: ABC and airway protection, decontamination (remove clothes, wash skin), **atropine** titrated until secretions dry and chest clears (it treats muscarinic features only), **oximes** (e.g. pralidoxime) may reactivate the enzyme before 'aging' — use per local protocol. Intensive care for respiratory failure. Intermediate syndrome (proximal and respiratory weakness at about 1–4 days) can follow.

steps.title: Safety and help
steps.body: Pesticide ingestion is an emergency — call 112. Many cases are intentional self-harm: after stabilisation, assess mental health and offer support (Tele-MANAS 14416).

steps.title: Targets
steps.body:
- **Cell wall**: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) bind penicillin-binding proteins → block transpeptidation; **vancomycin** binds D-Ala-D-Ala.
- **30S ribosome**: aminoglycosides (gentamicin — misreading, bactericidal), tetracyclines (block aminoacyl-tRNA).
- **50S ribosome**: macrolides (azithromycin), clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid.
- **DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV**: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin).
- **Folate synthesis**: sulfonamides (dihydropteroate synthase) + trimethoprim (DHFR) = co-trimoxazole.
- **RNA polymerase**: rifampicin. **Mycolic acid synthesis**: isoniazid.

steps.body:
- **Aminoglycosides**: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade.
- **Vancomycin**: nephrotoxicity, infusion reaction ('red man / vancomycin flushing syndrome').
- **Fluoroquinolones**: tendinopathy/tendon rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects; avoided in children/pregnancy generally.
- **Tetracyclines**: tooth discoloration and bone effects in children, photosensitivity; avoid in pregnancy.
- **Chloramphenicol**: aplastic anaemia, grey baby syndrome.
- **Isoniazid**: hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine prevents). **Rifampicin**: orange body fluids, hepatitis, enzyme induction. **Ethambutol**: optic neuritis (colour vision). **Pyrazinamide**: hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia.
- **Clindamycin** (and many broad-spectrum agents): *C. difficile* colitis.
- **Linezolid**: myelosuppression, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:

- **Calcium channel blockers**: dihydropyridines (amlodipine) dilate arterioles → ankle oedema; non-DHPs (verapamil, diltiazem) slow the heart.
- **Thiazides** (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone): Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter in DCT → hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperglycaemia.
- **Loop diuretics** (furosemide): Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ in thick ascending limb → oedema/heart failure; ototoxicity at high doses.
- **Potassium-sparing**: spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist; gynaecomastia), amiloride (ENaC).
- **β-blockers**, **α1 blockers**, central **α2 agonists**; **methyldopa**/labetalol/nifedipine are used in pregnancy.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Phases (left heart)
steps.body:
1. **Atrial systole** — tops up ventricular filling (more important at high heart rates or with stiff ventricles).
2. **Isovolumetric contraction** — ventricle contracts with all valves closed; pressure rises steeply. Begins with mitral closure (**S1**).
3. **Ejection** — aortic valve opens when LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (~80 mmHg); rapid then reduced ejection.
4. **Isovolumetric relaxation** — aortic valve closes (**S2**); pressure falls with all valves shut.
5. **Filling** — mitral valve opens; rapid filling (may give **S3**), diastasis, then atrial systole again (**S4** if the ventricle is stiff).

steps.title: Wiggers' diagram clues
steps.body: The **dicrotic notch** on the aortic pressure trace marks aortic valve closure. The jugular venous pulse shows **a** (atrial contraction), **c** (tricuspid bulging), **x** descent, **v** (venous filling), **y** descent (tricuspid opening).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying S1 is the opening of valves — heart sounds are caused by valve **closure** and associated vibrations.
- Forgetting that ventricular volume does not change during isovolumetric phases.

scenes.text: An ICU chart lists heart rate 72/min and stroke volume 70 mL.
Your resident asks for cardiac output, ejection fraction and MAP.
Calculate carefully — units matter.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · CO and EF
steps.body:
CO = HR × SV = 72 × 70 mL = 5,040 mL/min ≈ **5.0 L/min**.

If end-diastolic volume (EDV) = 120 mL and SV = 70 mL: EF = SV ÷ EDV = 70 ÷ 120 = **0.58 (58%)**. End-systolic volume = 120 − 70 = 50 mL.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Mean arterial pressure
steps.body:
At resting heart rate MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ (SBP − DBP).
BP 120/80: MAP = 80 + (40 ÷ 3) = **93 mmHg**.

Also MAP ≈ CO × total peripheral resistance (TPR), so a fall in CO with constant TPR lowers MAP.

steps.title: Regulation of stroke volume
steps.body:
- **Preload** (EDV) — Frank–Starling law: greater stretch → stronger contraction (up to a point).
- **Contractility** — sympathetic stimulation, catecholamines and inotropes raise it.
- **Afterload** — the pressure the ventricle must eject against (raised by hypertension, aortic stenosis).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert mL to L.
- Using the simple ⅓ formula for MAP at very high heart rates, where diastole is shorter and MAP lies closer to the arithmetic mean.

steps.title: Baroreceptor reflex
steps.body: Stretch receptors in the **carotid sinus** (afferent: glossopharyngeal) and **aortic arch** (afferent: vagus) fire less when pressure falls. The medulla responds with **less vagal** and **more sympathetic** output: tachycardia, increased contractility, arteriolar and venous constriction. This defends MAP — so a near-normal BP can hide significant blood loss.

steps.title: Hypovolaemic shock in physiology terms
steps.body: Loss of volume → ↓ venous return → ↓ preload → ↓ SV → ↓ CO. Compensation: tachycardia, vasoconstriction (cold skin, narrow pulse pressure), renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and ADH to retain water. Falling BP is a **late** sign.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: A bleeding patient with tachycardia needs immediate senior/trauma team help, haemorrhage control and fluid/blood resuscitation per protocol.

steps.title: Learning note

This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Volumes and capacities (typical young adult)
steps.body:
- Tidal volume (TV) ≈ 500 mL · Inspiratory reserve (IRV) ≈ 3,000 mL · Expiratory reserve (ERV) ≈ 1,100 mL · Residual volume (RV) ≈ 1,200 mL.
- **Vital capacity** = IRV + TV + ERV · **Functional residual capacity** = ERV + RV · **Total lung capacity** = VC + RV.

RV and therefore FRC and TLC **cannot be measured by simple spirometry** (helium dilution or body plethysmography is needed).

steps.title: Compliance and surfactant
steps.body: Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP. Low in fibrosis (stiff lungs), high in emphysema (loss of elastic recoil). **Surfactant** (from type II pneumocytes, mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) lowers surface tension, prevents alveolar collapse (Laplace: P = 2T/r) and increases compliance. Deficiency in preterm babies causes **respiratory distress syndrome**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling FRC a 'volume' — it is a capacity (sum of ERV and RV).
- Saying spirometry measures RV.

lessons.title: Lab: Ventilation and the alveolar gas equation

scenes.text: A patient breathes shallowly at 30/min with tidal volume 250 mL.
Is his alveolar ventilation as good as his minute ventilation suggests?
Work the numbers.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Alveolar ventilation
steps.body:
Alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × RR.

Normal: (500 − 150) × 12 = **4,200 mL/min** (minute ventilation 6,000).
Shallow fast: (250 − 150) × 30 = **3,000 mL/min** (minute ventilation 7,500!).

So rapid shallow breathing wastes more of each breath on dead space.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Alveolar gas equation
steps.body:
PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Patm − PH₂O) − PaCO₂ ÷ R.
At sea level, room air: 0.21 × (760 − 47) − 40 ÷ 0.8 = 149.7 − 50 ≈ **100 mmHg**.

If PaO₂ is 90 mmHg, A–a gradient ≈ **10 mmHg** (normal for a young adult). A raised gradient points to a lung problem (V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion defect) rather than pure hypoventilation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to subtract water vapour pressure (47 mmHg at 37 °C).
- Thinking hypoventilation raises the A–a gradient — it lowers PAO₂ and PaO₂ together, so the gradient stays normal.

steps.title: The O₂–Hb dissociation curve
steps.body: Sigmoid because of **cooperative binding**. P50 ≈ 26–27 mmHg. **Right shift** (lower affinity, more unloading): ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺ (Bohr effect), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG, exercise. **Left shift**: fetal haemoglobin, ↓temperature, alkalosis, **carbon monoxide**, methaemoglobin.

steps.title: Carbon monoxide
steps.body: CO binds haemoglobin about 200–250 times more avidly than O₂, reduces O₂-carrying capacity and shifts the curve left, so tissues get less O₂. PaO₂ (dissolved O₂) can be normal, and ordinary pulse oximeters read carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin. CO-oximetry on a blood gas is needed. Treatment: remove from source and give high-flow oxygen; severe cases need specialist care.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Never use charcoal or gas heaters in a closed room. Suspected poisoning: call **112**, move everyone to fresh air.

steps.title: Chemoreceptors
steps.body:
- **Central chemoreceptors** (ventral medulla) respond to **H⁺ in CSF**, which reflects arterial PCO₂ (CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier). They provide most of the drive from CO₂.
- **Peripheral chemoreceptors** (carotid and aortic bodies) respond mainly to **low PaO₂** (especially below ~60 mmHg), also to ↑PCO₂ and ↑H⁺. Carotid bodies signal via CN IX.

In some patients with chronic CO₂ retention, giving uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen can worsen hypercapnia (mainly through V/Q changes and the Haldane effect), so oxygen is titrated to a target saturation set by the team.

scenes.text: Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma a day.
Yet you pass only about 1.5 litres of urine.
Where does the rest go?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: GFR and Starling forces
steps.body: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (≈180 L/day). Net filtration pressure = (glomerular capillary hydrostatic − Bowman's space hydrostatic) − (glomerular oncotic − Bowman's oncotic). Afferent arteriole constriction lowers GFR; efferent constriction (angiotensin II) raises glomerular pressure and helps maintain GFR when perfusion falls.

steps.title: Tubular handling
steps.body:
- **PCT**: reabsorbs ~65% of Na⁺ and water, almost all glucose and amino acids (SGLT2, secondary active), most bicarbonate.
- **Thick ascending limb**: Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (blocked by loop diuretics); impermeable to water → dilutes tubular fluid and builds medullary gradient.
- **DCT**: Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter (blocked by thiazides).
- **Collecting duct**: aldosterone (Na⁺ reabsorption, K⁺/H⁺ secretion) and **ADH** (inserts aquaporin-2 → water reabsorption).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the descending limb pumps salt — it is water-permeable; the **ascending** limb pumps.

lessons.title: Lab: ABG interpretation step by step

scenes.text: A blood gas arrives: pH 7.21, PaCO₂ 25 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L.

steps.title: Five-step method
steps.body:
1. **pH**: < 7.35 acidaemia, > 7.45 alkalaemia.
2. **Primary process**: HCO₃⁻ low → metabolic acidosis; PaCO₂ high → respiratory acidosis (and vice versa for alkalosis).
3. **Compensation**: metabolic acidosis — Winter's formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2).
4. **Anion gap** = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal about 8–12 mmol/L (lab-dependent).
5. **Clinical cause**: high-gap (ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, toxins such as methanol or ethylene glycol, salicylates) or normal-gap (diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
pH 7.21 → acidaemia. HCO₃⁻ 10 → metabolic acidosis.
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 (21–25). Measured 25 → **appropriate respiratory compensation**.
Anion gap = 140 − (104 + 10) = **26** → high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling compensation 'complete' — the body rarely brings pH fully back to normal.
- Skipping the anion gap and missing a toxic cause.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body:
Hypothalamus → releasing hormone → anterior pituitary → trophic hormone → target gland → hormone, which **feeds back** to inhibit both hypothalamus and pituitary.

- TRH → TSH → T4/T3
- CRH → ACTH → cortisol
- GnRH → LH/FSH → sex steroids
- GHRH (and somatostatin inhibition) → GH → IGF-1
- Dopamine **inhibits** prolactin.

steps.title: Primary vs secondary
steps.body: **Primary** failure of a gland: low hormone, **high** trophic hormone (no feedback). **Secondary** (pituitary) failure: low hormone, low or inappropriately normal trophic hormone. Example: primary hypothyroidism → low free T4, high TSH.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that prolactin is under tonic **inhibition** — pituitary stalk damage raises prolactin.
- Reading TSH alone in suspected pituitary disease — TSH may be 'normal' when it should be high.

steps.title: Thyroid hormone
steps.body: Iodide trapped (Na⁺/I⁻ symporter) → oxidised and attached to tyrosine on thyroglobulin by **thyroid peroxidase** → mono- and di-iodotyrosine residues coupled to form T3/T4. T4 is converted to the more active T3 in tissues (deiodinases). Actions: ↑BMR, heat production, cardiac β-receptor sensitivity, brain development in infancy.

steps.title: Calcium control
steps.body: **PTH** (parathyroids) raises serum Ca²⁺: bone resorption, renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, phosphate excretion, and 1-α-hydroxylation of vitamin D (calcitriol → gut absorption). The parathyroids sit behind the thyroid and can be injured or devascularised at thyroidectomy → **hypocalcaemia**: perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs.

steps.title: When to escalate

steps.title: Insulin and glucagon
steps.body:
**Insulin** (β-cells; released when glucose enters via GLUT2, is metabolised, ATP closes K-ATP channels, Ca²⁺ enters): GLUT4 translocation in muscle and fat, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis, K⁺ entry into cells; inhibits lipolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis.

**Glucagon** (α-cells; released in fasting): glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver, ketogenesis. Counter-regulatory hormones also include adrenaline, cortisol and growth hormone.

This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Valid consent
steps.body: Capacity, voluntary, adequately informed: diagnosis, procedure, benefits, material risks (common and serious), alternatives including no treatment, in a language the patient understands; time to ask questions. The person consenting should be able to perform the procedure or be trained to consent for it.

steps.title: Pre-op assessment
steps.body: History (cardiac, respiratory, anaesthetic problems, bleeding, drugs especially anticoagulants, antiplatelets, diabetes medication), examination, ASA grade, investigations as indicated (not routine for all), fasting instructions per anaesthesia, VTE risk assessment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Consenting a patient who lacks capacity; not discussing alternatives; forgetting to plan anticoagulant management.

steps.title: Three phases
steps.body:
**Sign In** (before induction): identity, site marked, procedure, consent, anaesthesia safety check, pulse oximeter, allergies, airway/aspiration risk, blood-loss risk.
**Time Out** (before skin incision): team introduces itself, confirm patient, site, procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis, anticipated critical events, imaging displayed.
**Sign Out** (before patient leaves theatre): procedure recorded, instrument/swab/needle counts correct, specimen labelled, equipment problems, key recovery concerns.

steps.title: Culture
steps.body: Anyone in the team can stop the process if something doesn't match. Psychological safety saves lives.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rushing the Time Out as a ritual; site marking missing or washed off; counts reconciled after the patient has left; not voicing a concern because of hierarchy.

steps.title: Maintenance fluids (Holliday–Segar 4-2-1)
steps.body: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg + 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg + 1 mL/kg/h for each kg above 20. Adults are often prescribed ~25–30 mL/kg/day; include K, Na and glucose needs, and add losses (NG, drains). Always individualise (heart failure, renal disease, elderly).

steps.title: Post-op fever by timing (rough guide)
steps.body:
- Day 0–2: physiological response, atelectasis.
- Day 3–5: pneumonia, UTI, line infection.
- Day 5–7: anastomotic leak, wound infection, collection.
- Day 5+: DVT/PE.
Drugs and transfusion can cause fever at any time.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Tachycardia, rising CRP, peritonism or ileus after bowel surgery → suspect anastomotic leak; urgent senior review and CT.

scenes.text: A 50-year-old labourer notices a groin bulge on lifting.
Examine standing, then lying.

steps.title: Key points
steps.body: Examine standing: inspect, cough impulse, assess reducibility. Inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernia below and lateral. Indirect hernias pass through the deep ring (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels) and may descend to the scrotum; direct hernias bulge through Hesselbach's triangle (medial). Clinical distinction is imperfect; repair approach is similar.

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: Irreducible, tender, red hernia with obstruction signs → strangulation → urgent surgery. Femoral hernias have a higher strangulation risk.

steps.title: Presenting
steps.body: 'A reducible right-sided groin swelling with a cough impulse, above and medial to the pubic tubercle, consistent with an inguinal hernia; the other side is normal. I would like to examine the abdomen and scrotum.'

steps.title: Triple assessment
steps.body:
1. **Clinical** examination (with chaperone, respectful exposure, all quadrants, axilla).
2. **Imaging:** mammography (older women) and/or ultrasound (younger women, dense breasts).
3. **Tissue:** core needle biopsy (or FNA).
Concordance between all three is reassuring; any suspicious element needs MDT discussion.

steps.title: Communication
steps.body: Explain each step, address fear, avoid premature reassurance, give a timeline and a named contact. Encourage breast awareness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the axilla and the other breast; not offering a chaperone; promising 'it's nothing' before results; relying on one normal test when the other two are suspicious.

steps.title: Before you suture
steps.body: Check tetanus status, neurovascular status distal to wound, foreign bodies (consider X-ray for glass), wound contamination. Irrigate well. Local anaesthetic per protocol with maximum dose awareness.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Enter at 90°, equal bites each side, evert edges, tie with instrument tie (square knots), don't over-tighten, space sutures evenly. Remove sutures by site (face earlier, limbs later) per local guidance.

steps.title: Refer instead of suturing
steps.body: Tendon, nerve or vessel injury, joint involvement, heavily contaminated or bite wounds, facial cosmetic areas or wounds needing exploration — escalate to a senior or the appropriate specialty.
